name: Creole nationalism
summary: Creole nationalism is the ideology of American-born colonial elites, above all in Spanish America around 1808-1826, who turned grievances over exclusion from office and imperial extraction into a demand for independent nationhood under their own leadership. It combined Enlightenment republicanism, a distinct American patriotism and Catholic symbols with a reluctance to share power with Indigenous, mixed-race and enslaved majorities.
scope: The Spanish American independence-era creole movement (Bolivar, Hidalgo, Iturbide, Miranda, San Martin) and its early-republic continuation, following Anderson's idea of creole pioneers. It does not cover later Caribbean, African or Indonesian creole movements, or modern mestizo nationalism.

sources.usedFor: War methods, slavery and Church positions, monarchist and republican options, caudillos.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Early-19th-century creole elites had no health-care programme; any view would be projected from later states, so this is unaddressed.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Wage regulation was foreign to a landed creole elite running an unfree and tribute-based labour system; inferred from its class interests.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Creoles attacked Spanish trade monopolies but also relied on state, Church and estate privileges, so no consistent market doctrine is documented.

public-ownership.rationale: Creole leaders confiscated royalist property but did not advocate public ownership of utilities; inferred from landowning and mercantile interests.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Creoles were themselves the colonial wealthy and resented Crown taxation; no record of seeking higher taxes on their own class.

unions-good.rationale: Modern labour unions did not exist; inferred from an elite that kept hierarchical labour relations after independence.

property-fundamental.rationale: Creole landowners and merchants fought partly to hold property and offices against Crown exactions, and the republics they founded protected estates.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Corporations in the modern sense were absent; the nearest issue, Spanish monopoly companies, was opposed, but this is not a regulatory stance.

cut-welfare.rationale: No welfare state existed; Church charity was the model, and creole writers did not debate cutting it.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not raised; creole elites kept haciendas and mines under owner control, so inferred opposed.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Anachronistic; independence governments used police and loyalty tests on royalists but no source frames it around terrorism.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Not an issue of the independence era and no source addresses it.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Anachronistic; patriot press promoted Enlightenment free expression but also hostile rhetoric against peninsulares and Indigenous people.

strong-leader.rationale: Bolívar and Iturbide built strong executives, and Bolívar expected single-man rule in places, reflecting the creole preference for order over gridlock.

state-harmful.rationale: Creole nationalists wanted to seize and run the state themselves, so the idea of a stateless society is foreign to the programme.

limit-guns.rationale: Creole-led armies and militias were the means of independence; inferred opposed to disarmament, though not a stated policy.

empower-police-military.rationale: New republics leaned heavily on armies and caudillos for order after independence, but funding of forces was not a stated programme.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Catholic moral norms prevailed among creoles; not discussed in sources, inferred from that culture.

decide-locally.rationale: Creoles split: Bolívar warned that large states drift toward empire and favoured republics of manageable size, while others built centralist states, and federalists fought centralists.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal doctrine is not discussed in the sources; Enlightenment-influenced reformers and punitive caudillos both appear.

traditional-family.rationale: Creole society was Catholic and patriarchal with families central to elite status, though sources do not state a family doctrine.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Inferred from the Catholic, patriarchal creole culture; the question is anachronistic.

abortion-legal.rationale: Inferred from Catholic creole culture; not discussed.

more-religion-public.rationale: Creole identity drew on Catholic symbols such as the Virgin of Guadalupe, and Iturbide's Plan of Iguala made the Church a pillar of the new state.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Creole nationalists largely gave little weight to Indigenous and mixed-race majorities and protected their own place at the top of the casta order.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Anachronistic; the Catholic creole elite held conventional gender views, so inferred disagreement.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Creoles built a distinct American identity, for instance idealising an Aztec or Inca past while keeping Spanish-descended culture.

gradual-change.rationale: Creoles chose rupture with Spain through civil war, though many wanted post-independence social structures preserved.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Early republics often wanted European immigrants but resented peninsulares, so no uniform position is documented.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: No international bodies existed; Bolívar sought a union of American states and European backing but kept sovereignty, so inferred mildly opposed.

free-trade.rationale: Bolívar condemned Spanish trade restrictions and monopolies, and independence opened trade to Britain, though protection for local interests also appeared.

nation-first.rationale: Creole nationalism put the interests of the new American nation over the Spanish empire, though Bolívar also pursued pan-American union.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The concept is anachronistic; Bolívar did call on Europe to intervene on behalf of American independence.

open-borders.rationale: New republics had defined territories and loyalty tests; open borders was not part of the programme.

limit-growth.rationale: Anachronistic; Bolívar imagined commercial emporia and growth, so inferred opposed.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Enlightenment-influenced elites valued progress, but no source states a view on technology solving problems.

revolution-justified.rationale: Creole nationalism is defined by revolt against Spanish authority, and Bolívar's letter justifies armed independence against colonial rule.

experts-over-public.rationale: Creole elites doubted the readiness of the broad population, and Bolívar said citizens lacked political virtues, but no statement about experts.

central-planning.rationale: Not an issue; creole economic complaint was monopoly, and inferred opposition to planning follows from that.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not addressed; owner-controlled estates and trade were the elite model.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Creole families protected estates and entails; inferred opposed.

basic-income.rationale: Anachronistic; elite creole politics had no such concept.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Creoles split between trade opening and protecting local manufacture, with views varying by region and period.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Not a stated creole position; Bourbon colonial planning was disliked but new states used state-directed projects.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Creole elites kept great estates and did not push wide small ownership; inferred.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Not addressed; strongly inconsistent with a landowning and mercantile elite.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Not addressed; guild and Church corporations existed under Spain but creoles did not propose state wage bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: Post-independence politics grew through elections, parties and newspapers, though strongmen dominated; no one-party doctrine.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Patriots backed either monarchies or republics; Iturbide set up a Mexican Empire, but Bolívar opposed American monarchies.

democracy-best.rationale: Bolívar doubted that Americans were ready for full representative government, and creole rule often meant narrow elite republics.

direct-votes.rationale: Creole republican thought favoured representatives and congresses; direct lawmaking not documented.

workers-councils.rationale: Not an issue; contrary to elite creole republicanism.

right-to-secede.rationale: Creoles claimed the right to leave the Spanish empire but opposed breakup of their own new states, as Bolívar's Gran Colombia shows.

natural-rulers.rationale: Creoles asserted that American-born elites were fit to govern against peninsulares, while doubting the masses, though the claim was framed as birthright.

political-violence-never.rationale: Creole independence came through civil wars, and Bolívar's war to the death policy is documented.

war-builds-character.rationale: No source states the view; the heroic independence wars produced a cult of founders, but also warnings about violence.

separate-church-state.rationale: Plan of Iguala concentrated power in the creole elite and Church, though liberals later fought for separation.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Creoles were Catholic but wrote modern constitutions influenced by the Enlightenment, not scripture-based law.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Not addressed; creole leaders built state armies.

military-superiority.rationale: Not stated; creoles wanted armies to win independence and keep order, but rivalry among new states is undocumented in sources.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Creoles defined nation by birth in the Americas and not purely by descent, with Bolívar saying Americans are neither Indians nor Europeans; but whites kept privilege.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Creole elites stopped backing insurrection when it radicalised the lower classes.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Inferred: creoles defended their rank in a hierarchical casta society.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Creole nationalists largely excluded Indigenous peoples from the nation, though some tribute and encomienda reforms were promised.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Bolívar blamed Spanish rule for American misfortune, but reparations are not an issue in sources.

civilizational-union.rationale: Bolívar urged union of the countries of the Americas in the Jamaica Letter and pursued the Federation of the Andes.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Not addressed; mercantile rivalry with peninsulares drove some grievances, but the movement was framed as patriotism.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Republican virtue was stressed by Bolívar, but creoles also invoked the rights of Americans against Spain.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The independence-era sources show no creole debate on nature's intrinsic worth, so there is no basis for a stated position.

limit-population.rationale: Creole nationalists wrote of peopling and developing the Americas, never of limiting population; no stated position.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from elite faith in commerce and progress.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Nothing in the creole independence literature concerns speeding up technological change at the cost of institutions.

human-enhancement.rationale: Bodily enhancement by technology lies wholly outside the concerns of 1810s patriots.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Cryptography as a civil liberty is far beyond the creole era; patriots did use ciphers, but took no stand on it.

restore-past-order.rationale: Creoles sought a new order of independent states, though they conserved many colonial social features, culturally if not legally.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Not stated; Bolívar was pragmatic about suiting institutions to circumstances, but this is not a creole doctrine.

direct-action.rationale: Creoles used juntas, congresses and elections as well as arms; direct action is not their doctrine.

means-match-ends.rationale: Creole leaders fought wars to build republics and did not debate whether methods should mirror the intended society.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Inferred from the elite's idealisation of civic progress; not documented.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Not addressed; contrary to creole hierarchical society.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from elite property interests.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Inferred rejection by a landowning and mercantile elite.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Alien to creole elites, who feared lower-class radicalisation.

collective-farming.rationale: Not addressed; opposed to estate and smallholder agriculture.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Not addressed; Bolívar thought republics were not imperialistic and that Europe had trade interests in helping independence.

taxation-theft.rationale: Creoles resented Crown extraction but their republics levied taxes.

harm-principle.rationale: Creoles drew on Enlightenment liberty but their sources do not state the harm principle as a limit on state power.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Creoles invoked Enlightenment rights while defending corporate and caste privileges.

conscription.rationale: Patriot armies recruited heavily, including casta soldiers promised social improvement, though no doctrine is stated.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Inferred; creoles sought self-rule, not exit.

state-as-business.rationale: Creole nationalists wanted to take over the state as a sovereign republic, not to run it like a firm serving customers.

positive-liberty.rationale: The Jamaica Letter speaks of freedom from Spanish tyranny, not of material means as a condition of freedom.

media-academia-power.rationale: Anachronistic; creole nationalism grew through newspapers and pamphlets, but no claim about their power.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Casta ideology ranked Spanish descent above others and Peruvian press rhetoric was openly racist, so inferred; scientific racism was later.

organic-representation.rationale: Corporate representation was colonial practice; creole republicans mostly adopted party and congressional politics.

national-rebirth.rationale: Rhetoric of an American nation shedding Spanish rule and recovering an indigenous past had a rebirth tone, but this is inferred.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Bolívar argued republics have no cause to expand, yet he built large states.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Caudillismo had personal loyalty features, but creole nationalism argued from nation and republic.

bound-labor.rationale: Colonial labour institutions such as encomienda and tribute persisted for some time, but creoles did not defend them as a doctrine.

universal-morality.rationale: Enlightenment natural rights ideas inspired the independence era, but this is not detailed in the sources.

single-common-good.rationale: Creole republicans spoke of the patria's interest but the sources show elite factions competing, so no doctrine of a single reasoned good.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The question belongs to a different nationalism and creole sources never touch it.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Creole nationalists had no diaspora to recall; their concern was American-born people already in the territory.

revive-national-language.rationale: Creoles spoke Spanish and Portuguese and used them as national languages, with no revival projects.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Not addressed; opposed by owner interests.

school-vouchers.rationale: Education in the creole era was Church-run or state-run, so vouchers were not an issue.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Stimulus economics postdates the era; new republics borrowed abroad out of need rather than doctrine.

economic-freedom.rationale: Anti-monopoly grievance suggests belief in economic freedom, but sources do not link it to political freedom.

rule-by-example.rationale: Bolívar stressed civic virtue, but not rule by example over law.

national-self-determination.rationale: The defining claim: Bolívar and the creole patriots demanded independent nationhood for the Americas against European rule.

force-without-un.rationale: No international body with a security council existed; patriots simply sought foreign support for their cause.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Creoles were Enlightenment-influenced but retained Catholic faith and Church ties.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Poor relief was a Church matter in the colonies, and creole nationalists did not discuss limiting it by citizenship.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Welfare conditionality is a modern debate; creole sources have nothing on it.

class-collaboration.rationale: Creole nationalism asked all classes to unite behind the nation, though it excluded Indigenous people; inferred.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Not addressed; Creole nationalists valued a heritage including Spanish and Indigenous pasts.

dominated-front.rationale: Bolívar urged American union and sought European help against Spain, so a front among dominated Americans fits.

workers-nation.rationale: Anachronistic; nationalism was framed around elite creole citizens.

ban-interest.rationale: Not addressed; mercantile creoles used credit.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Creole independence did not legislate segregation, but the casta hierarchy had legal ranking before; republics used equality in law in principle.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Creole writers did not analyse the state as a class instrument; they saw Spain's rule as foreign domination instead.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Fossil fuel policy is anachronistic for the independence era.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The sources do not say how creole nationalists wanted newcomers to relate to the national culture.

elite-replacement.rationale: The replacement-by-immigration claim is a modern conspiracy theory with no counterpart in creole nationalism.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral formulae were not an issue for the early congresses and juntas the sources describe.

national-mission.rationale: Bolívar thought Americans needed northern political virtues, not spread their own system, though the letter also hopes for American liberty.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Creole grievance targeted peninsular officials who took office from creoles and Spain's extraction of wealth.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenic policy came later than the creole independence movement.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Accountability for security-force abuses was not a creole concern; the patriots themselves waged a war to the death.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Creole leaders built states with large ambitions and kept Church and military roles.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Casta order privileged Spanish descent and creoles feared sharing power with mestizos, though Bolívar called Americans a mixture.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Creoles invoked Enlightenment equality against Spain while defending casta rank, so adherents split.

socialism-one-country.rationale: The question concerns Marxist-Leninist debates that creole nationalists never joined.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Creoles saw themselves as native Americans against Spanish usurpers, as Bolívar's letter puts it, not as colonists.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Not addressed; corporate privileges (fueros) persisted for some time.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Creole society was uniformly Catholic, so conversion law was not a live issue in the sources.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Irrelevant to creole culture; cattle economy of the Americas.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Church education was the norm; inferred.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: This is a Soviet-era doctrine with no link to creole nationalism.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Patriots justified independence by American peoples' own authority after the Spanish crown's collapse, with juntas and congresses, though consent was elite-limited.

trade-surplus.rationale: Creoles attacked Spanish monopoly rather than formulating a balance-of-trade doctrine, so no stated view.

population-transfer.rationale: Not documented; Bolívar's war to death targeted peninsulares by status.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Creole independence wars initiated armed action against Spanish authority.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: The creole sources do not frame history as competition between peoples driving progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Parties barely existed in the independence wars, and outlawing them was not discussed.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Bolívar's complaint that Spain made Americans serfs fit for work reflects the idea that being under foreign power is itself unfree.

separated-powers.rationale: Early republican constitutions in the independence era adopted Enlightenment-based divisions of power.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Elite creoles gave little weight to the poor majority; inferred.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council housing is a modern British policy, outside the creole world.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Industrial strikes were not a feature of the creole-era economy.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Creole writers blamed Spanish misrule, not population growth, for American hardship.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Creole nationalists were uneasy about mestizo and Indigenous majorities but Bolívar celebrated mixture.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Not a republican creole proposal; elections and appointment were the practice.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Creole leaders used martial rule and extraordinary measures such as the war to the death against enemies; inferred as general stance.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Colonial authorities set food prices, but the sources give no creole position on it.

party-controls-media.rationale: Patriot movements depended on a free press and pamphlets.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not a creole concept; caudillos commanded armies directly.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: The sources do not record creole positions on naturalisation periods.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Elite creole politicians were not ascetic paid representatives; inferred.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party discipline was irrelevant to juntas and congresses of the period.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Bolívar proposed confederation of American states, yet nationalists defended independence; split.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Bolívar and Iturbide concentrated executive and military control; strong presidents were common after independence.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Not addressed beyond the Church's alliance with creole elites.

clerical-rule.rationale: Creole priests led revolts, but clerical rule was not the aim.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Inferred; nationalists backed the national cause.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The patriot press was a nationalist tool, but censorship of art for virtue is not documented as a creole stance.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Bolívar favoured life presidency in his constitution plans, and caudillos kept power, so a leader remaining long was accepted.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall of officials is not recorded in creole independence-era constitutions the sources discuss.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Patriots sought alliances, with Britain especially, and Bolívar appealed to Europe.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Not addressed; contrary to propertied creole interests.

people-in-arms.rationale: Patriot militias existed but Bolívar built regular armies.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Not addressed; elite creoles held both rural estates and city posts.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Bolívar pursued unity of former viceroyalty territories in Gran Colombia and the Andes federation.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Creole nationalists were themselves the educated elite, including lawyers and priests.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Creole elites ranked cultures and castes, with some Peruvian rhetoric openly racist; inferred.

death-penalty.rationale: Patriot leaders executed royalists, including Bolívar's war to the death; inferred.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The evolution dispute did not exist in the independence era.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The creole claim rests on birth in the Americas, not descent from Spain, so birth-based membership is closer; adherents were still descended from Spanish settlers.

minority-language-support.rationale: Creole nationalism gave little weight to Indigenous groups and promoted Spanish; inferred.

religious-exemptions.rationale: With one established Catholic church, creole nationalists faced no question of minority exemptions.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Not addressed; new republics borrowed from Britain.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Creoles sought to end Spanish monopoly and open trade but largely preserved social structures culturally if not legally.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Congress of Chilpancingo and other patriot congresses wrote independence declarations and constitutions.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Rapid economic development as a justification for curbing freedoms is a modern doctrine, absent from the sources.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Bolívar wanted European support for independence, but duties of aid to the poor are not stated.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear weapons postdate the creole era.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Bolívar favoured life presidency; creole constitutions varied.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central banks as independent institutions were not part of the creole independence debate.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial bargaining for peace is not discussed in the creole sources.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Not addressed; creoles defended property but also confiscated royalist estates.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: This is a debate within Marxism that creole nationalism never addressed.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation was not a concern for creole nationalists.

collective-defense.rationale: Patriot states cooperated militarily against Spain, and Bolívar called for American union and European backing.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The sources do not give a creole doctrine on annexation without consent.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Creoles were hurt by Bourbon attacks on Church power and later the Church backed creole elites; liberals pushed the other way.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Whether a head of state should stand above parties was not debated in the sources; Iturbide and Bolívar were openly partisan leaders.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Creole-led states used force to keep territory together, as in the Mexican and Central American civil wars.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Special autonomy for a region joining a larger state was not a creole concern.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Creoles rejected monarchy as a source of legitimacy, so a divine ruler is contrary, though Iturbide became emperor.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Income taxation did not exist in the independence-era economy.

character-from-environment.rationale: Bolívar blamed Spanish despotism for forming Americans into serfs unready for freedom, an environmental view.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Creole movement opposed Crown arbitrariness, though its strongmen later ruled by decree.

space-expansion.rationale: Space travel is wholly outside the creole era.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Bolívar admired the British model with a hereditary senate and strong executive, but this letter excerpt does not state it.

leader-cult.rationale: Cult of founders such as Bolívar and utopian nationalist fiction fed national feeling in the republics.

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody presumptions were not discussed by creole nationalists.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: This is a debate inside socialism; creole nationalism has no view.

land-redistribution.rationale: Creole elites held great estates; Hidalgo's radical agrarian following frightened them, and many creoles backed off.

refugee-return.rationale: The sources record no creole position on return of displaced people.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Creoles defined nations by colonial territories rather than by kin abroad.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Not addressed; Catholic confessional states existed.

women-must-cover.rationale: Not part of the Catholic creole culture.

common-currency.rationale: Bolívar wanted American union, but no source shows a shared currency as a goal.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Bolívar spoke of Americans as a common people and urged union.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Not addressed; creoles excluded Indigenous groups instead of granting autonomy.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The question concerns persecuted minorities choosing emigration, a topic outside creole nationalism.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Not addressed; creole interests in office and trade were material, but nationalism was framed in ideas.

ban-cartels.rationale: Bolívar attacked monopoly in the Spanish trade system.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bank and firm bailouts did not exist as a policy choice in the creole era.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The sources do not show creole nationalists debating judicial limits on majorities.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Creoles attacked exclusive imperial trade systems; Bolívar wanted open trade.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding labour and environmental trade standards are modern policy, absent from the creole record.

moral-incentives.rationale: Bolívar stressed civic virtue, but incentives were not discussed.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Creole independence leaders raised armies and fought, not waiting for conditions.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Creoles resented peninsular privilege but many kept titles, entails and church or military fueros after independence.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Creole nationalism produced national histories and glorified an Indigenous past, such as the Aztec and Inca.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Creole elites treated Indigenous people as needing guidance, but they opposed Spain's own claim to tutelage.

patriotic-education.rationale: Creole nationalism expanded through pamphlets and press that cultivated national feeling.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Anachronistic; the question assumes modern policies.

public-money-creation.rationale: Money creation by a public body is a modern monetary reform not found in the creole sources.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Creole sources contain no theory of capitalist crises.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Patriots sought to end Spanish influence entirely, and Mexico's Brading-noted nationalism rejected the former rule.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: This Marxist concept has no counterpart in creole nationalism.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Discrimination law is a modern issue; the creole sources do not address it.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Congress declarations existed, but entrenched bills of rights were not a creole doctrine.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: The sources give no creole position on colonial treaties dividing a people.

elective-rulers.rationale: Republics chose rulers by election among the political nation, though some patriots, such as Iturbide, preferred a monarch.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The creole case against Spain was that the Crown and its peninsular officials broke the compact with Americans, which justified resistance.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Patriot congresses, such as Chilpancingo, held sovereign authority in the independence era.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Animal welfare was not discussed by creole nationalists.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Creole estates raised livestock without any recorded debate on humane limits.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Catholic elite paternalism was typical, inferred rather than documented here.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Creoles were politically engaged, seeking office and sovereignty.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: The Frankfurt-school critique of mass culture has no counterpart in creole nationalism.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: The Gramscian idea of hegemony is absent; creole sources treat Spanish rule as force and monopoly.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Creole grievances against Spain stressed the extraction of colonial wealth.

native-born-offices.rationale: The creole grievance was exclusion from offices held by peninsulares, and nationalism demanded offices for American-born; Bolívar notes Americans rarely held high posts.

party-own-road.rationale: The question concerns relations between communist parties, far from creole nationalism.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Not addressed; patriots sought British loans and help.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The sources record no creole demand for territory lost in a war.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Creole nationalists sought creole control of the new nations, giving Indigenous and mixed people little weight.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Fascism postdates creole nationalism by over a century.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: The comparison of fascism and communism is a twentieth-century debate.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: The American Civil War question is not part of creole nationalist debate.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Debates over monuments of condemned figures are modern and absent from the sources.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Programmes for boys and men facing disadvantage are a modern policy debate, with no creole counterpart.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: This question is modern; creole sources do not touch domestic violence policy.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Bolívar argued that Americans differ from Europeans and North Americans, so institutions had to fit their circumstances and readiness.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Armies and their leaders became arbiters in the new republics, and Bolívar expected military rule in places.

paid-care-work.rationale: Paying for domestic labour was foreign to a society where such work was done by women of the household or by servants and slaves.

office-by-exam.rationale: Not addressed; creoles wanted offices for themselves rather than a merit system.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Creoles sought to open trade, and the sources record no policy of blocking foreign purchases of firms.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Not addressed; elite representation by congress.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension systems did not exist in the creole era.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Creole elites held private estates; inferred opposed.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Patriot congresses claimed fiscal powers against the Crown, but not documented in sources.

single-official-language.rationale: Creole nationalism treated Spanish and Portuguese as national languages and largely excluded Indigenous languages from public life.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The sources show no creole restriction on land ownership by foreigners.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Disparate-impact doctrine is a modern legal idea, and creole elites defended the casta hierarchy rather than test policies for racial outcomes.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Creole writers did not criticise consumption; Bolívar even looked forward to commercial emporia.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Patriots sought foreign backing and Bolívar blamed Europe for not helping, but arming insurgents abroad was not doctrine.

corporate-influence.rationale: Corporate lobbying is modern, though creoles did resent the influence of Spanish merchant monopolies.

restrict-foreign-funding.rationale: NGO funding rules are modern; creole patriots themselves relied on foreign money and arms.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: The sources show no creole population policy of paying families to have children.

residents-only-property.rationale: Local property purchase limits are not discussed in the creole sources.

job-guarantee.rationale: Guaranteed public employment is a modern idea, and creole elites would not have backed it.

democratic-peace.rationale: Bolívar argued republics are not imperialistic, a related but different claim.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Creole leaders legitimised new authorities and demanded obedience from royalists.

non-intervention.rationale: Creole nationalism claimed that Spain had no right to rule the Americas, which supports non-intervention by outside powers, though Bolívar sought European aid.

industrial-unions.rationale: Industrial unions did not exist in the creole era.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Not documented, though peninsulares were cast as hostile.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Freedom of information laws are modern, and creole sources do not state a view.

local-production.rationale: The creole case was for open commerce, so localist production is not a stated position.

informal-organisation.rationale: Creoles organised in juntas, congresses and armies.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Sovereignty from Spain was the point; inferred.

religious-nation.rationale: Catholicism was part of creole identity in Mexico, but nations were defined by place of birth rather than shared religion.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Creole nationalism was rejecting submission to the Spanish crown and its tribute.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Not addressed; some regional creole elites resented the centre.

defeat-communism.rationale: Communism did not exist as a state doctrine during the creole independence era.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Mixed provision of public services is a modern debate outside creole sources.

religion-illusion.rationale: Creole identity relied on Catholic symbols and clergy such as Hidalgo.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Creole writers praised commerce and trade but did not theorise capitalism as historically progressive.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Women's equality was not a creole concern in the independence era.

socialized-care.rationale: Public provision of childcare is modern, and Catholic creole households kept care private.

purge-loanwords.rationale: No language purism in the sources; creoles kept Spanish and Portuguese.

treaties-binding.rationale: Treaties with nations within borders are not part of creole nationalism, which excluded Indigenous nations from the political community.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Small commons-owning communities were not a creole aim; the movement wanted large republics ruled by elites.

majority-settlement.rationale: The sources record no creole policy of settling majority-group members in minority regions.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Creole nationalism predates both, so a third course between them is not at issue.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Creoles invoked American birth and, in Bolívar's letter, descent from the land's first owners to claim the territory against Spanish usurpers.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The Holocaust postdates creole nationalism, which has no position on it and no basis for denial.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Patriot regimes suppressed royalists and strongmen later suppressed rivals.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Catholic confessional states in early independence, but inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The core grievance, stated by Bolívar, was that Spain treated America as a source of tribute and monopoly profit.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: The question concerns Islamic doctrine and is irrelevant to Catholic creole nationalism.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Creoles did not fight rulers for being irreligious; they fought for independence from the Spanish crown.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The sources show elite congresses and juntas, with no doctrine of direct popular participation in workplaces and universities.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Intersectional analysis is modern, and creole elites tended to defend casta and gender hierarchies.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The question is modern and contrary to the conservative Catholic culture of the creole elite.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: The left-right division itself emerged later in the Americas, so this is not a creole concern.

alienated-labor.rationale: The Marxist notion of alienation is absent, and creole elites relied on bound and tribute labour.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Creole nationalism has no recorded position on Islam and the West.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Patriots grounded authority in the people of the colony and the juntas after the king's fall, not in God.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: Employment confidentiality agreements are modern, with no creole counterpart.

social-market-economy.rationale: The social market model is a postwar European idea, which creole nationalism did not address.

rich-first.rationale: No source records a creole view on letting some regions get rich first.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Not addressed; patriots sought British help.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Iturbide's empire sought dynastic monarchy, but Bolívar opposed it for the Americas.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: Mutual credit banks were not part of creole programmes.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Austerity conditionality by the IMF postdates the creole era, though new republics soon fell into debts to British lenders.

property-franchise.rationale: Early creole-run republics limited citizenship and the vote, and Bolívar doubted that all Americans had the political virtue for representation.

domination-women-nature.rationale: Ecofeminism is modern; creole nationalists held conventional views on women.

reification.rationale: This Marxist concept is not found in creole nationalist writing.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Patriot press was a creole tool; the claim is Marxist.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Constitutional republics vs arbitrary Crown rule, inferred.

racial-franchise.rationale: Creoles defended white privilege in practice but republics generally avoided explicit racial franchise.

online-participation.rationale: Internet deliberation is a modern question absent from the sources.

open-government-data.rationale: Open government records are a modern transparency issue, outside the creole sources.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Catholic marriage law applied; not addressed.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: The sources record no creole campaign against shops owned by a religious minority.

citizens-assembly.rationale: Sortition-based assemblies are modern; creole patriots used elected congresses and juntas.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Creoles generally kept Catholic doctrine as it stood, and the sources do not mention reinterpretation for modern conditions.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Creole elites were the wealthy; but Bolívar warned that aristocracies would be rejected.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Open service by gay and lesbian soldiers is a modern policy, and creole Catholic culture would have rejected it.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Contrary to the Catholic creole identity.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Creoles feared sharing power with Indigenous people and mestizos, as in Mexico.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Church charity was the typical colonial welfare institution; inferred.

term-limits.rationale: Bolívar favoured a life presidency and caudillos extended rule.

vote-delegation.rationale: Liquid delegation of votes is a modern idea with no creole counterpart.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Extinction risk as a policy priority is a recent concern.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: The creole movement's Catholic culture reserved Church offices for men.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: The sources do not record creole views on voting rights for foreign residents.

rent-control.rationale: Rent caps did not figure in the creole independence debate, and property-owning elites would have been against them.

abolish-ip.rationale: Patents and copyright were minor issues in the creole era.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Drilled youth movements are a twentieth-century feature, not part of creole nationalism.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Inferred from the rejection of foreign rule.

recognise-genocide.rationale: The sources record no creole stance on recognising genocide.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Peruvian creole nationalism glorified an Inca past, and Mexican creoles idealised an Aztec one, to claim continuity for the new nation.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: The idea that sex is socially constructed is modern and contrary to creole views.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Feminist theory on the category of women is modern, and creole society held fixed gender roles.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: The independence wars generated heroes and a cult of founders.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Creole nationalism was a political and commercial struggle, with only some Catholic symbolism, so no stated view.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: The sources show no diaspora concept in creole nationalism.

culture-before-state.rationale: Creole nationalism sought political independence and state control first.

god-not-male.rationale: Creole Catholicism used traditional male language for God.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Feminist scriptural criticism is modern and absent from the creole sources.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Creoles resented peninsular merchants' mercantile control and wanted the economy in native hands.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Creoles drew states along colonial administrative lines, not by merging regions by people.

independent-unions.rationale: Unions did not exist in the independence era.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The question concerns the definition of socialism, which creole nationalists never discussed.

local-essentials-public.rationale: The sources show no creole position on public ownership of water, hospitals or transport.

second-chamber.rationale: Bolívar proposed a hereditary or life senate in his later constitutions, inferred; other creoles also bicameral.

municipal-property.rationale: Community ownership of production was not a creole programme, which defended private estates.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Bolívar envisaged confederation of states, but towns confederation not discussed.

family-wage.rationale: The sources record no creole position on wages sufficient to support a family.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Drug regulation did not exist in the independence era.

ageing-research-funding.rationale: Life-extension research is far outside the creole era.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Untraceable digital payments are a modern issue.

online-anonymity.rationale: Online anonymity is a modern issue with no creole counterpart.

person-over-state.rationale: Creole writers invoked rights against Spain but did not state a personalist principle about the person and the state.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Federalist and centralist creoles fought over this, but the sources do not give a settled creole answer.

gm-crops.rationale: Genetic engineering postdates the creole era.

dense-cities.rationale: Urban density and the environment were not creole concerns.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Creoles organised for creole interests, but the group was defined by birthplace and status.

racial-pride.rationale: Elite creoles took pride in Spanish ancestry while asserting a distinct American identity; inferred.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Creoles fought wars of independence, which they cast as defensive, and later wars of expansion.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Creole nations shared a language with Spain but defined themselves as separate peoples by birth and territory.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: The sources record no creole claim of foreign plots to partition their countries, though Bolívar feared European designs and division among the new states.

free-public-college.rationale: Higher education was Church-linked and elite in the creole era, with no tuition debate recorded.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Pollution taxation is a modern idea, absent from creole sources.

future-generations.rationale: Obligations to future generations about the environment are modern and not stated in creole sources.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Creole sources record no theory of women's distinct public values.

arms-reduction.rationale: Creole states built armies to win and defend independence, so arms reductions were not an aim, though no source states a view.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Patriot leaders negotiated with Britain and others in private, and the sources show no commitment to open diplomacy.

capital-controls.rationale: Capital movement controls are not discussed in the creole sources.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Inferred; the new states sought to monopolise force under caudillos.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Creole nationalists depended on soldiers obeying orders in the independence wars, so refusal runs against the cause.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Collective bargaining is modern and unrecorded in creole sources.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Tax credits for low-paid families are modern policy.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Inferred from grievance with trade monopoly.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Creoles aimed to replace Spanish colonial administration with their own, rather than inherit it.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Creoles sought uniform national institutions rather than letting communities try different economic systems, but no source states it.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Natural capital accounting is a modern idea, though creole writers prized American resources as sources of wealth.

sacred-nation.rationale: Creole nationalism treated the American patria as a cause; some, in Mexico, saw creoles as a chosen people.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Student loans did not exist in the creole era.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Creoles rejected the idea of themselves as colonised, while Indigenous people could claim it against them.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The Enlightenment influenced creoles but sources do not state a doctrine of a fixed shared human nature.

public-service-media.rationale: Publicly funded independent media did not exist, and patriot newspapers served the cause.

farm-price-support.rationale: Crop price guarantees are not discussed in the creole sources.

workers-own-party.rationale: Workers' parties came later than the creole elites' own politics.

ban-fgm.rationale: Female genital mutilation was not an issue in creole society.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The sources show no creole position on women's inheritance, which colonial Spanish law partly allowed already.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Language-naming disputes are not part of creole nationalism, which used Spanish and Portuguese as they were.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Property-based pollution liability is a modern libertarian proposal absent from the creole sources.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Indigenous authorities were marginalised by creole nationalists.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Environmental trade-offs with liberty are not a creole issue.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Sentencing rules are not discussed in the creole sources.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The sources show no creole language requirement for immigrants, though Spanish dominated public life.

delink-world-market.rationale: Creoles wanted trade opened to Britain and Europe after Spanish monopoly ended, as Bolívar's letter anticipates, so breaking ties is inferred opposed.

communal-electorates.rationale: Creole republics adopted territorial representation, and caste or corporate electorates were not their aim; inferred from the congresses they convened.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Anachronistic; no creole source addresses binding fiscal rules.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: Anachronistic: modern unions did not exist in the independence era, and no view is documented.

voter-id.rationale: Anachronistic; creole republics limited suffrage by property and literacy rather than ID, and no stance on ID is documented.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Creole movements fused Catholic symbols such as Guadalupe with patriotism and kept Catholicism as the state religion, so no equal standing for other interpretations.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Creole leaders mixed republican elections with strong executives and restricted suffrage; adherents did not hold a settled view on this definition.

premarital-sex.rationale: Inferred from the Catholic social norms of the creole elite; the sources do not discuss it.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: Anachronistic: no stance can be documented for an independence-era movement.

negative-income-tax.rationale: Inferred from the landed creole elite's interests and the absence of any welfare state in the period.

women-suffrage.rationale: Independence-era republics did not give women the vote, and Bolivar's writings address male citizens; inferred from period practice.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Inferred from the movement's Catholic allegiance and the Church's central role in creole identity.

race-social-construct.rationale: The creole elite defended a caste hierarchy and feared Indigenous, mixed-race and enslaved majorities, inferred as not seeing race as constructed.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the elite's patriarchal order, with no documented position.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Inferred: creole elites were landowners, but the sources do not discuss a first-claim theory of property.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Inferred and anachronistic: international criminal courts did not exist in the independence era, and creole leaders prized national sovereignty.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred: creole patriots were Catholic but Enlightenment-influenced, and the sources show no stance on literal scripture reading.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Inferred from the creole elites' reluctance to share power with Indigenous and mixed-race majorities, which makes guaranteed gender equality in group self-rule unlikely.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Anachronistic and inferred: planned economies came later, and creole republicans favoured property-owning republics.

indirect-election.rationale: Inferred from the elite-led, restricted-franchise republicanism of the period, which preferred filtered selection of higher offices.

national-church-status.rationale: Inferred from the Catholic symbols and identity the creole movement used and the early republics' Catholic establishment.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Inferred from creole reluctance to share power with Indigenous majorities, which makes ethnic territorial autonomy unlikely.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Inferred: creole leaders claimed self-determination for their own nation, but did not hold a general doctrine of local votes on territory.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: The independence states largely kept the colonial administrative boundaries under uti possidetis rather than redrawing them.

simple-living.rationale: Inferred: creole elites sought commercial opening and prosperity, not austerity.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Inferred from creole elites' reluctance to share power with Indigenous majorities and desire to open land to settlement.

equal-conscription.rationale: Inferred and anachronistic: the independence-era debate about militias did not address women's conscription.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Bolivar's letter presents Americans as a distinct people with a claim to their native land, but the sources record no spiritual or duty language.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Anachronistic: drug policing is not addressed by any source, and the wars of independence saw both summary violence and appeals to legality.

close-ties-china.rationale: Anachronistic: China is not addressed in the independence-era sources.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The sources record no policy toward kin abroad.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Inferred from a landowning creole elite whose interests lay in private property and who resisted redistribution; no source addresses common ownership.

self-ownership.rationale: Split: Enlightenment republicanism supports individual liberty, but creole elites often kept slavery and bonded labour.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Inferred from creole resentment of imperial extraction under the Bourbon reforms; the sources do not mention consumption taxes specifically.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Anachronistic: targeted versus universal social spending is not addressed.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Early republics produced both party-like factions and caudillo rule; no consistent position is recorded.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Bolivar attacks the Spanish trade monopoly and exclusion from office as favouritism for the mother country, from which opposition to privileged firms is inferred.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Catholic symbols such as the Virgin of Guadalupe were central and the Church kept privileges in the early republics, so strict separation of religion and politics is inferred to be rejected.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Anachronistic: technology and ancestral values are not addressed.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Inferred from Catholic, patriarchal colonial society; no source addresses divorce.

national-resource-control.rationale: Bolivar's letter complains that Spain monopolised the colonies' wealth and trade, and creoles sought control of American resources for Americans.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Anachronistic: no source addresses theories of just distribution.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Anachronistic: financial transaction taxes are not addressed.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Creole elites were reluctant to share power with Indigenous, mixed-race and enslaved majorities, but sources do not frame this as a view on racism today.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Bolivar justifies rejecting Spanish rule as illegitimate usurpation, from which the view that unjust rule lacks authority is inferred.

multipolar-world.rationale: Bolivar's letter argues for American union and independence from Spain but does not set out a multipolar world order.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Anachronistic and inferred: a landowning elite is unlikely to have held that labour creates value.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Creole patriotism served elites who were reluctant to share power with the majority, so its fit with worker politics is inferred to be weak.

material-over-identity.rationale: Anachronistic: the left's priorities are not addressed.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Anachronistic: inferred from republican and monarchist options debated in the period, not communist party rule.

missingStatements.text: Public offices and trade should be reserved for those born in the country rather than for officials sent from the mother country.
missingStatements.rationale: The peninsular monopoly of high office was the central creole grievance.

missingStatements.text: A people born in a colony may rightly claim the land as their own against the imperial power that settled it.
missingStatements.rationale: Bolívar describes Americans as heirs of the land's first owners against Spanish usurpers.
missingStatements.declined: Covered loosely by indigenous-land-authority and historical-land-claim; the creole claim is specific to colonial history.

notes: Strands differ: Hidalgo's insurgency had a popular and agrarian wing that creole elites feared, Iturbide chose monarchy, Bolívar republic with strong executive. Most answers outside independence, office, trade and race are inferred and low confidence.
